prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Now spring appears, with beauty crowned And all is light and life around, Why comes not Jane? When friendship calls, Why leaves she not Augusta’s walls? Where cooling zephyrs faintly blow, Nor spread the cheering, healthful glow That glides through each awakened vein, As skimming o’er the spacious plain, We look around with joyous eye, And view no boundaries but the sky. Already April’s reign is o’er, Her evening tints delight no more; No more the violet scents the gale, No more the mist o’erspreads the vale; The lovely queen of smiles and tears, Who gave thee birth, no more appears; But blushing May, with brow serene, And vestments of a livelier green, Commands the winged choir to sing, And with wild notes the meadows ring. O come! ere all the train is gone, No more to hail thy twenty-one; That age which higher honour shares, And well become the wreath it wears. From lassitude and cities flee, And breathe the air of heaven, with me.

outputs.L1:
Now spring appears, with beauty crowned,  
And all is light and life around.  
Why comes not Jane? When friendship calls,  
Why leaves she not Augusta’s walls,  
Where cooling zephyrs faintly blow,  
Nor spread the cheering, healthful glow  
That glides through each awakened vein  
As, skimming o’er the spacious plain,  
We look around with joyous eye  
And view no boundaries but the sky?

Already April’s reign is o’er;  
Her evening tints delight no more.  
No more the violet scents the gale;  
No more the mist o’erspreads the vale.  
The lovely queen of smiles and tears,  
Who gave thee birth, no more appears;  
But blushing May, with brow serene  
And vestments of a livelier green,  
Commands the wingèd choir to sing,  
And with wild notes the meadows ring.

O come, ere all the train is gone,  
No more to hail thy twenty-one—  
That age which higher honour shares  
And well becomes the wreath it wears.  
From lassitude and cities flee,  
And breathe the air of heaven with me.
outputs.L2:
Spring has arrived in all its splendour, filling the world with brightness and vitality—yet Jane is still absent. Why, when a friend invites her, does she remain within Augusta’s walls? There, the weak breezes bring neither refreshing coolness nor the invigorating warmth that courses through every newly awakened vein when we sweep across the broad countryside, gazing happily upon a landscape whose only limit is the sky.

April has already ended. Its glowing sunsets, violet-scented winds, and mists drifting over the valley have vanished. That charming sovereign of mingled sunshine and showers—the month in which you were born—has departed. In its place, calm-browed May appears, rosy and dressed in richer green, calling the birds to song and filling the fields with their untamed music.

Come before the whole procession of spring has passed and can no longer celebrate your twenty-first year—an age of greater distinction, well suited to the garland it bears. Leave weariness and city life behind, and join me beneath the open sky, where we may breathe heaven’s own air.
outputs.L3:
Spring has arrived, filling the countryside with beauty, light, and renewed life. In the midst of this awakening, the speaker wonders why Jane still remains within the walls of Augusta rather than answering the affectionate call of friendship.

The delicate signs of April—the violets, soft mists, and muted evening colors—have already begun to fade. In their place, May has brought brighter greenery, warmer skies, and the joyful music of birds. Jane is therefore urged to come quickly, before the freshness of spring passes away. Her visit would also offer a fitting opportunity to celebrate her arrival at the honorable age of twenty-one.

Above all, the speaker invites Jane to leave behind the fatigue and confinement of urban life. In the healthful open air of the countryside, the two friends can enjoy nature’s beauty, welcome the new season, and share in one another’s companionship.
outputs.L4:
Why do you still linger in Augusta, Jane, when the city has grown so dull and weary? Leave its dusty streets, oppressive heat, and tiresome routines behind, and come away into the countryside, where spring has filled the world with beauty. The woods are green, the fields are bright with flowers, and the open air offers freedom, freshness, and renewed health. Here, beneath the clear sky and among the songs of birds, you may cast off every care and recover the happiness that city life has diminished.

April has already passed, and May is slipping quickly away. The loveliest part of the year will not wait for us, and soon its blossoms, breezes, and radiant days will be gone. Come, then, before spring gives way to summer. Come celebrate your twenty-first birthday in nature, surrounded by all that is youthful, joyful, and alive. Do not let this brief season vanish while you remain shut within Augusta; escape while its pleasures are still ours to enjoy.
outputs.L5:
**Now, And, Why**

Now is the moment we live in—the brief space between memory and possibility. It asks us to pay attention, to notice what is happening before it becomes the past.

And is the word that connects. It reminds us that life is rarely one thing or another. We can be hopeful and afraid, strong and uncertain, content and still eager to grow.

Why is the question that leads us deeper. It challenges habits, uncovers meaning, and pushes us to understand ourselves and the world around us.

Together, these three words offer a simple guide: live **now**, connect with **and**, and never stop asking **why**.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a rhyming poem inviting a young woman named Jane to leave the city and enjoy the spring countryside in celebration of her twenty-first birthday.
counterfactuals.output:
Dear Jane, leave the city with its clamor and its light,  
And wander where the fields awake in green and gold delight.  
The larks will sing above us, and the dancing streams will run,  
While blossoms lift their faces to the warm and waking sun.  

Come trade the crowded pavements for a path through hawthorn trees,  
The traffic’s restless rumble for the whisper of the breeze.  
We’ll picnic by the river where the willow branches sway,  
And toast your twenty-first beneath the gentle skies of May.  

For spring has spread her ribbons over meadow, hill, and glen,  
And twenty-one comes only once—it will not come again.  
So leave the town behind you; let the countryside be seen—  
Happy birthday, dearest Jane, the springtime’s birthday queen!
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Regency-era verse in which Augusta urges her friend Jane to visit before May ends, contrasting unhealthy city life with fresh country air.
counterfactuals.output:
**Augusta to Jane**

Dear Jane, ere yet the bloom of May  
In summer’s brighter breath decay,  
Forsake the town’s oppressive glare,  
Its smoky streets and languid air.  

What health can crowded squares bestow,  
Where lamps at noon seem scarce to glow,  
And every rout, though gayly dress’d,  
Leaves aching head and sleepless breast?  

Come where the hawthorn scents the lane,  
And larks awake the verdant plain;  
Here crystal brooks through meadows stray,  
And roses promise June’s display.  

No stifling coach, no midnight ball,  
No cards, nor tiresome morning call—  
But wholesome winds, a quiet seat,  
And friendship’s converse, ever sweet.  

Then, dearest Jane, no more delay:  
Pray quit the town before ’tis May;  
Ere its last tender evening flee,  
Come breathe the country air with me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a pastoral birthday poem with April, May, violets, zephyrs, meadows, and a “winged choir,” written in an elegant early nineteenth-century style.
counterfactuals.output:
When April, weeping, yields her place  
To May’s young smile and sunnier grace,  
And violets, from their mossy bed,  
In modest blue the meadows spread;  

When fragrant zephyrs softly stray  
Through budding boughs at close of day,  
And, hidden in the woodland spire,  
Awakes the joyous wingèd choir—  

Then comes thy natal morn, as bright  
As dew-drops in the tender light;  
And Nature, robed in green and gold,  
Seems all her blessings to unfold.  

May every year that crowns thy brow  
Bring peace as pure as breathes there now;  
May Hope beside thy pathway stay,  
And Love make every season May.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an affectionate poetic invitation addressed to Jane, asking why she remains within Augusta’s walls when spring has arrived and friendship calls.
counterfactuals.output:
**To Jane**

Why linger, Jane, in Augusta’s walls,  
When spring unbinds the streams and flowers?  
The thrush is singing, friendship calls  
Beyond the gate, beyond the towers.

Come where the tender woodlands gleam,  
And hawthorn scents the wandering air;  
We’ll follow paths beside the stream,  
And make the brightening hours more fair.

Leave stone and shadow—come away!  
The fields await your welcome tread;  
For friendship, warm as newborn day,  
Has set the green world wide ahead.
